(p-309) Surah al-Fath

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

The first: We have informed you with clear knowledge concerning what We sent down to you of the Qur'an and what We commanded you with of the religion.

Knowledge is sometimes expressed by "conquest" (fath), as in His statement ﴿And with Him are the keys (mafatih) of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am: 59], meaning the knowledge of the unseen, as said by Ibn Bahr.

And as in His statement ﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has certainly come to you﴾ [al-Anfal: 19], meaning: if you seek knowledge, then knowledge has certainly come to you.

The second: We have decided for you a clear decision concerning what We have opened for you of the lands.

Concerning what is meant by this conquest there are two opinions:

The first: the conquest of Makkah, which Allah promised him in the year of al-Hudaybiyah when he turned back from it.

The second: it is what occurred in his affair at al-Hudaybiyah.

al-Sha'bi said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest﴾ [al-Fath: 1] was revealed at the time of al-Hudaybiyah, in which he attained what he had not attained in any other.

The Pledge of Ridwan was made, they were fed the palm trees of Khaybar, the Romans prevailed over the Persians in confirmation of his report, and the sacrificial animal reached its place of sacrifice. Accordingly, what he intended by the conquest is the day of al-Hudaybiyah. Jabir said: "We did not count the conquest of Makkah except as the day of al-Hudaybiyah."

The second: it is the Pledge of Ridwan.

al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "You count the conquest as the conquest of Makkah, while we count the conquest as the Pledge of Ridwan on the day of al-Hudaybiyah."

The third: it is his sacrificing and shaving his head on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, until the sacrificial animal reached its place of sacrifice through the slaughter.

Al-Hudaybiyah is a well, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rinsed his mouth in it; it had dried up, then it gushed forth with water.

﴿That Allah may forgive you your past sins and those to come﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects:

The first: that Allah may forgive you, completing His favors upon you.

The second: that He may make you patient over the harm of your people.

Concerning it there are three sayings:

The first: what preceded the conquest and what came after the conquest.

The second: what preceded prophethood and what came after prophethood.

The third: what has occurred and what has not occurred, by way of promise that it is forgiven when it happens.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: what preceded the revelation of this verse and what came after it.

﴿And complete His favor upon you﴾. Concerning it there are two sayings:

The first: by the conquest of Makkah, al-Ta'if and Khaybar.

The second: by the submission of those who were arrogant and the obedience of those who were tyrannical.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾ ﴿and help you with a mighty help﴾. It may bear two meanings:

The first: that it is capture and spoils, as it was on the day of Badr.

The second: that it is victory, Islam, and the conquest of Makkah.

The cause of the revelation of this verse is what al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the statement was revealed: ﴿Nor do I know what will be done with me or with you﴾, the people of Makkah said: 'O Muhammad, how can we enter your religion when you do not know what will be done with you or with those who follow you? Why did he not inform you of what will be done with you and with those who follow you, as 'Isa ibn Maryam informed?' This weighed heavily upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions until he came to Madinah. Then 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the leader of the hypocrites, said to the Ansar: 'How will you enter the religion of a man who does not know what will be done with him or with those who follow him? By Allah, this is manifest error.'

Then Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you not ask your Lord to inform you of what will be done with you and with those who follow you?' He said: 'Indeed, for Him there is a term; so rejoice in what will delight your eyes.'

Until these verses were revealed to him while he was in the house of Abu al-Dahdah, at a meal with Abu Bakr and 'Umar. He went out and recited them to his companions. One of them said: 'Congratulations and good cheer, O Messenger of Allah! Allah has explained to us what will be done with you; so what will be done with us?' Then Allah revealed: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and remove from them their misdeeds﴾, the verse."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 4–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility (al-sakinah) into the hearts of the believers﴾. On it there are three interpretations:

First: it is patience in the command of Allah.

Second: it is certainty in the promise of Allah.

Third: it is mercy for the servants of Allah.

﴿That they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ may carry three interpretations:

First: that they may increase in action alongside their affirmation (of faith).

Second: that they may increase in patience alongside their striving.

(p-312) Third: that they may increase in confidence in victory alongside their faith in the reward.

﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ may carry two interpretations:

One of them: its meaning is: And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, as an encouragement for the believers toward the good of this world and the reward of the Hereafter.

The second: its meaning is: And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, to make the believers aware that in their struggle they have helpers in obeying their Lord.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who harbour an evil thought about Allah﴾. On it there are four interpretations:

First: it is their thought that Allah has a partner.

Second: it is their thought that Allah will never send anyone (as a messenger).

Third: it is their thought that Allah would make them like His Messenger (i.e., that they would be killed).

Fourth: that He would give them victory over His Messenger.

Al-Dahhak said: The tribes of Asad and Ghatafan thought about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah that he would be killed or defeated and would not return to Madinah safely, but he returned victorious.

﴿Upon them is the cycle of evil﴾ may carry two interpretations:

One of them: upon them revolves the evil of their belief.

The second: upon them revolves the requital for what they believed about their Prophet.

First, a witness over your community concerning the delivery of the message. This is the view of Qatadah.

Second, a witness over your community concerning their deeds, whether obedience or disobedience.

(p-313) ﴿and a bringer of good news and a warner﴾: this has two interpretations.

First, a bringer of good news to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers.

Second, a bringer of good news of Paradise to whoever obeys, and a warner of the Fire to whoever disobeys. This is the view of Qatadah. Good news and warning together are better, because one who informs of a pleasing matter is a bringer of good news, and one who cautions against a disliked matter is a warner.

al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani said:

"Those who recite charms have warded it off because of its evil course; they release it at times, and at times they turn it back."

The words ﴿and you may support him﴾ (wa-tu'azzirūhu) have three interpretations.

First, you obey him. This is said by some of the people of lexicography (ahl al-lughah, the scholars of Arabic language).

Second, you venerate him. This is said by al-Hasan and al-Kalbi.

Third, you help him and defend him against harm. From this comes ta'zir (discretionary correction) in the prescribed punishments (hudud), because it prevents. This is said by al-Qatami:

"Has Mayy not come early in the morning without folly, reproaching, while the beloved is benefited by rebuke?"

As for ﴿and honour him﴾ (wa-tuwaqqirūhu), there are two interpretations.

First, you make him a master (sayyid, a lord or chief). This is said by al-Suddi.

Second, its interpretation varies according to their disagreement about who is referred to by this mention. Some said that what is meant by ﴿and support him and honour him﴾ is: you support God and honour Him, because His saying ﴿and glorify Him﴾ refers to God, and so does what precedes it. On this view, the interpretation of ﴿and honour him﴾ is: you affirm for Him the validity of lordship (rububiyyah) and deny that He has a son or a partner.

Others said: what is meant by it is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that they support him and honour him, since his mention has preceded. So it is permissible that some of the speech refers to God and some of it refers to His Messenger. This is said by al-Dahhak.

On this view, the interpretation of ﴿and honour him﴾ is: you call him by his prophethood and messengership, not by his personal name or kunyah (patronymic).

﴿and glorify Him﴾ (wa-tusabbihūhu) has two interpretations.

First, glorifying Him by declaring Him free of every blemish.

Second, it is the performance of the prayer in which there is glorification (tasbih).

The poet said:

"By my life, you are indeed the House: I honour its people, and I sit in its shade in the evenings."

The poet said:

The second: destroyed (hālikīn). This was said by Mujahid.

Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:

"Length of years does not benefit men of foolishness, and God guides the path of the ruined (būr) folk."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 18–19:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾. The cause of this pledge, which is the Pledge of Ridwan (the Pledge of Good Pleasure), was the delay of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in Makkah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent him from al-Hudaybiyah as an envoy to the Quraysh. He was late in returning, and it was rumoured that he had been killed. So the Prophet ﷺ pledged allegiance with his companions, and they pledged to him to be steadfast and to fight. According to what Ibn Abbas narrated, they numbered one thousand five hundred. Jabir said they were one thousand four hundred. Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa said they were one thousand three hundred.

The pledge took place under the tree at al-Hudaybiyah, and the tree was a samurah (a kind of acacia tree).

It was named the Pledge of Ridwan because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree; so He knew what was in their hearts﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

The first: it refers to the sincerity of intention. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second: it refers to their dislike of the pledge, that they would fight with him until death. This was said by Muqatil.

﴿So He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

The first: the conquest of Khaybar, because of its nearness to al-Hudaybiyah. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: the conquest of Makkah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 20–24:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has promised you much booty that you will take﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: it refers to the spoils of Khaybar. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: it refers to every spoil that the Muslims would acquire. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿So He hastened this for you﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: it refers to the spoils of Khaybar. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the Treaty of Hudaybiyah. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: the Jews restrained their hands from Madinah when they went out to Hudaybiyah.

The second: the Quraysh restrained their hands from Madinah when they went out to Hudaybiyah.

The third: the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, the allies, led by Uyaynah ibn Hisn and Malik ibn Awf, came to support the people of Khaybar, but Allah cast terror into their hearts and they fled.

﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

One: that the restraining of their hands from you may be a sign for the believers.

The second: that the conquest of Khaybar may be a sign, i.e., a proof of the truthfulness of Allah the Exalted in His promise and of the truthfulness of His Messenger in his report.

It has been said: so that the Pledge (al-bay'ah) may be a sign for them.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And other [spoils] you were not able to obtain, but Allah has already encompassed them﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions: (p-318) One: they are the land of Persia, the Byzantines, and all that the Muslims would conquer. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they are Makkah. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: they are the land of Khaybar. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning His words ﴿Allah has already encompassed them﴾ there are two meanings:

One: Allah has power over them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: He preserved them for you so that their conquest would belong to you.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿[This is] the way of Allah which has already occurred among those before, and you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾. This means: the custom of Allah and His established practice in the past is the granting of victory to His messengers and His allies over their enemies.

Concerning His words ﴿And you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾ there are two meanings:

One: the way of Allah and His practice of granting you victory over your enemies and His enemies will not change.

The second: you will not find anything preventing the practice of Allah in granting victory to His messengers over their enemies, and this is a possible meaning.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them within the valley of Makkah﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects:

One: He restrained their hands from you through terror, and your hands from them through prohibition.

The second: He restrained their hands from you through abandonment, and your hands from them through sparing them, due to His knowledge of the condition of those among them who would embrace Islam.

The third: He restrained their hands from you and your hands from them through the peace treaty in the year of Hudaybiyah.

Concerning ﴿within the valley of Makkah﴾ there are two views:

One: by it He means Makkah.

The second: by it He means Hudaybiyah, because part of it is attached to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram).

Concerning His words ﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He gave you victory over them through the conquest of Makkah, and this verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah. It contains evidence that Makkah was conquered by peace treaty, based on His words ﴿restrained their hands from you and your hands from them﴾.

The second: He gave you victory over them through the fulfilment of the 'umrah from which they had prevented you.

The third: He gave you victory over them through what Thabit narrated from Anas: "Eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions from the direction of al-Tan'im at the time of the dawn prayer, intending to kill whomever they could seize. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) captured them and set them free, so Allah revealed this verse, and this was the victory."

The second: He restrained their hands from you through abandonment, and your hands from them through sparing them, due to His knowledge of the condition of those among them who would embrace Islam.

The third: He restrained their hands from you and your hands from them through the peace treaty in the year of Hudaybiyah.

Concerning ﴿within the valley of Makkah﴾ there are two views:

One: by it He means Makkah.

The second: by it He means Hudaybiyah, because part of it is attached to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram).

Concerning His words ﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He gave you victory over them through the conquest of Makkah, and this verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah. It contains evidence that Makkah was conquered by peace treaty, based on His words ﴿restrained their hands from you and your hands from them﴾.

The second: He gave you victory over them through the fulfilment of the 'umrah from which they had prevented you.

The third: He gave you victory over them through what Thabit narrated from Anas: "Eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions from the direction of al-Tan'im at the time of the dawn prayer, intending to kill whomever they could seize. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) captured them and set them free, so Allah revealed this verse, and this was the victory."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 20–24:

One: it refers to the spoils of Khaybar. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: it refers to every spoil that the Muslims would acquire. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿So He hastened this for you﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: it refers to the spoils of Khaybar. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the Treaty of Hudaybiyah. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: the Jews restrained their hands from Madinah when they went out to Hudaybiyah.

The second: the Quraysh restrained their hands from Madinah when they went out to Hudaybiyah.

The third: the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, the allies, led by Uyaynah ibn Hisn and Malik ibn Awf, came to support the people of Khaybar, but Allah cast terror into their hearts and they fled.

﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

One: that the restraining of their hands from you may be a sign for the believers.

The second: that the conquest of Khaybar may be a sign, i.e., a proof of the truthfulness of Allah the Exalted in His promise and of the truthfulness of His Messenger in his report.

It has been said: so that the Pledge (al-bay'ah) may be a sign for them.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And other [spoils] you were not able to obtain, but Allah has already encompassed them﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions: (p-318) One: they are the land of Persia, the Byzantines, and all that the Muslims would conquer. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they are Makkah. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: they are the land of Khaybar. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning His words ﴿Allah has already encompassed them﴾ there are two meanings:

One: Allah has power over them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: He preserved them for you so that their conquest would belong to you.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿[This is] the way of Allah which has already occurred among those before, and you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾. This means: the custom of Allah and His established practice in the past is the granting of victory to His messengers and His allies over their enemies.

Concerning His words ﴿And you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾ there are two meanings:

One: the way of Allah and His practice of granting you victory over your enemies and His enemies will not change.

The second: you will not find anything preventing the practice of Allah in granting victory to His messengers over their enemies, and this is a possible meaning.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 25–26:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They are those who disbelieved﴾, meaning the Quraysh.

﴿And they barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning they prevented you from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, when the Prophet ﷺ entered the state of ihram with his Companions for ʿUmrah.

﴿And the offering detained from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾. Regarding maʿkūfan (detained) there are three interpretations:

First: confined.

Second: standing still.

Third: gathered together. This was said by Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ.

﴿From reaching its place of sacrifice (maḥill)﴾. Regarding maḥill there are two views:

First: its place of slaughter (manḥar), as said by al-Farrāʾ.

Second: the Sacred Area (al-Ḥaram). This was said by al-Shafiʿi. The maḥill with a kasra on the ḥāʾ is the furthest point of a thing, and with a fatḥa it is the place where people alight. The offering consisted of seventy camels.

(p-320) ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know﴾, i.e., you did not know their faith.

﴿That you might trample them﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: that you might trample them with your horses and feet and so kill them, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: were it not for those believing men and believing women who were in the loins of the disbelievers and in the wombs of their women, whom they did not know, lest you trample their fathers and their children perish, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

﴿Then there would befall you from them a grievous burden﴾. Concerning maʿarrah (grievous burden) there are six sayings:

First: sin, as said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: the payment of blood money, as said by Ibn Ishaq.

Third: the expiation for accidental killing, as said by al-Kalbi.

Fourth: hardship, as said by Qutrub.

Fifth: blame.

Sixth: grief.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Had they been separated﴾. Regarding tazayyalū (separated) there are three interpretations:

First: had they been distinguished, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Second: had they been dispersed, as said by al-Kalbi.

Third: had they been removed, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, so that no Muslim would be mixed with the polytheists of Makkah.

﴿We would have punished those of them who disbelieved with a painful punishment﴾, which is killing by the sword, but Allah repels the disbelievers through the believers.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿When those who disbelieved had placed in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of ignorance﴾, meaning the Quraysh.

Regarding ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah (the zealotry of ignorance) there are two views:

First: partisanship for their gods which they worshipped besides Allah, and their aversion to worshipping anything else, as said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: their aversion to acknowledging his prophethood and to opening with "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" as he was accustomed to do in al-Fatihah, and their preventing him from entering Makkah, as said by al-Zuhri.

It may also bear a third meaning: imitation of their forefathers, and not opposing them in their customs, nor committing themselves to obeying others, as Allah related of them: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾, meaning the patience they showed, their acceptance of what they asked for, and the treaty they concluded, until he returned to them in the same month of the following year, as one who had completed his ʿUmrah and attained his objective.

﴿And He made them adhere to the word of piety﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations:

First: the statement "There is no god but Allah," as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ.

Second: sincerity, as said by Mujahid.

Third: the statement "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," as said by al-Zuhri.

Fourth: their saying "We hear and we obey," after their dispute.

It was called the word of piety because by it they guard themselves against the anger of Allah.

﴿And they were more deserving of it and worthy of it﴾. This may bear two meanings:

First: they were more deserving of the word of piety, to say it.

Second: they were more deserving of Makkah, to enter it.

Regarding who was more deserving of the word of piety there are two views:

First: the people of Makkah were more deserving of the word of piety to say it, due to the precedence of their warning, had it not been for the success that was withheld from them.

Second: the people of Madinah were more deserving of the word of piety when they said it, due to the precedence of their faith, when success accompanied them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 48, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth. You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and [hair] shortened.﴾ Qatadah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in a dream that he was entering Makkah in this manner. When he made the treaty with the Quraysh at al-Hudaybiyah, the hypocrites doubted, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (I did not see [this] in this year)."

Then He said: ﴿So He knew what you did not know﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: He knew that entering it would be after a year, and you did not know this. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: He knew that there were believing men and believing women in Makkah whom you did not know; and the verse [continues].

Then He said: ﴿So He made, besides that, a near victory﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: that it is the treaty that took place between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Quraysh at al-Hudaybiyah. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the conquest of Makkah. This was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak.

Regarding His saying: ﴿You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills﴾ there are three aspects:

The first: that it comes in the form of a condition and an exception (istithna') [i.e., "if Allah wills" is a conditional qualification].

The second: that it is not a true condition, but came in the form of a report, according to the custom of the people of religion (ahl al-din), and its meaning is: you will enter it by the will of Allah.

The third: "if Allah wills" refers to the entry of all of you or some of you, and because He knew that some of them would die.

Regarding His saying: ﴿You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills﴾ there are three aspects:

The first: that it comes in the form of a condition and an exception (istithna') [i.e., "if Allah wills" is a conditional qualification].

The second: that it is not a true condition, but came in the form of a report, according to the custom of the people of religion (ahl al-din), and its meaning is: you will enter it by the will of Allah.

The third: "if Allah wills" refers to the entry of all of you or some of you, and because He knew that some of them would die.

The first of them: it is the dust of the earth and the moisture of ablution (wudu), said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: it is their prayer appearing on their faces, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is the (serene) bearing (al-samt), said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: it is humility (khushu'), said by Mujahid.

The fifth: it is that one stays awake at night and so in the morning becomes yellowish, said by al-Dahhak.

The sixth: it is a light that appears on their faces on the Day of Resurrection, said by 'Atiyya al-'Awfi.

﴿That is their likeness in the Torah, and their likeness in the Gospel: like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: their likeness in the Torah is that their mark is on their faces,

and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot.

The second: both matters are their likeness in the Torah and their likeness in the Gospel.

As for His saying ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾, there are three opinions concerning it:

One of them: the shat' (shoot) is the thorn of the ear of grain (shawk al-sunbul), and the Arabs also call it al-safa and al-buhmi, said by Qutrub.

The second: it is the ear of grain (sunbul), so that from a single grain there come out ten ears, or nine, or eight, said by al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.

The third: it is its offshoots which come out from its sides; and from this comes shati' al-nahr, meaning the side of the river, said by al-Akhfash.

﴿So it strengthened it﴾ concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: so it equalled it, and became like its mother, said by al-Suddi.

The second: so it aided it, and the offshoots of the crop bound the roots of the plant and strengthened them.

﴿So it became thick﴾, meaning the gathering of the offshoots together with the roots.

﴿So it stood firm upon its stalk﴾, i.e., upon its stem on which it stands, so that it becomes its trunk.

﴿It pleases the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, because what pleased the believers of their strength, like the pleasure of the sowers at the strength of their crop, is what enraged the disbelievers among them.

As for the reason for striking this likeness with this crop which sends out its shoot: when the Prophet (ﷺ) began calling to his religion, he was weak; then he was answered one after another until his community grew and his affair became strong, like the crop that appears after the seed, weak, and then grows stronger state after state until its stalk and its offshoots become thick. This is among the most accurate of parables and the clearest of explanations.

And Allah knows best.
